title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Water
description: Curated OT/ICS cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

_otthreatfeed.usage: Free to reuse with attribution. Credit 'Mike Holcomb & UtilSec' and link back to otthreatfeed.com and to each item's linked primary source. Summaries are editorial paraphrase - verify against the primary source before acting.

items.title: Iran-linked hackers locked operators out of control panels at small Midwest water stations, the Wall Street Journal reports, as DHS tells Congress that water is increasingly in Iran-backed hackers’ sights
items.content_text: The Wall Street Journal reported on 13 November, citing unnamed US and Israeli officials, that since the summer Iran-linked hackers have locked operators out of control panels at water stations in small Midwestern towns. No utility, state or date has been named. Check Point’s Sergey Shykevich linked the activity mainly to CyberAv3ngers, which works under Iran’s cyber command, and acting CISA head Nick Andersen named programmable logic controllers as the equipment at risk. On 18 November DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin’s written testimony to the House Homeland Security Committee said Iran-backed actors have targeted US critical infrastructure since February, with water increasingly in their sights, mostly through localized disruptions of poorly secured control systems. Iran’s ambassador to France denies that Iran carries out cyberattacks abroad. It leads as the clearest official signal that exposed water controllers are the target (editorial assessment).

_otthreatfeed.category: Top Story

items.title: Illinois investigates an apparent cyberattack attempt on the Algonquin Dam on the Fox River
items.content_text: The Illinois Department of Natural Resources said on 20 November that its Office of Water Resources detected an apparent attempted cyberattack on the Algonquin Dam on the Fox River, about 45 miles northwest of Chicago, on 16 November. Staff blocked the unauthorised access at once, and IDNR says the dam stayed secure and fully operational. It has not said which system was targeted or whether gate controls were reachable. Illinois State Police, the Illinois Emergency Management Agency, the state’s technology department and CISA are assisting; IDNR says it has no indication of a link to other recent incidents, and no group has been named. For water-resource and flood-control owners, it is a prompt to check who can reach gate and level controls remotely (editorial assessment).

items.title: Switzerland confirms its first AI-agent cyberattacks: four of five succeeded, and a water operator was among the critical-infrastructure targets
items.content_text: Switzerland’s Federal Office for Cybersecurity (BACS) said on 26 November that five attacks in recent days used AI agents, tools that find weaknesses and plan next steps largely on their own. Four of the five compromised systems. Three targets were critical-infrastructure operators, which public broadcaster SRF identified as electricity, water and telecommunications providers. BACS named no victims or attacker and has not said whether any control systems were reached. The entry points were ordinary: default or easily guessed passwords and known flaws in internet-facing systems. On 24 November the UK NCSC reported a marked rise in such attacks since September, and a 13 November FBI IC3 advisory warned of misuse of the ARTEX framework. For small utilities with exposed PLCs and remote-access portals, the time to fix them is shrinking (editorial assessment).
tags: Incident — AI-agent-driven intrusions at Swiss companies and critical-infrastructure operators, including a water provider (BACS, 26 Nov 2026); whether IT or OT systems were hit is not disclosed; UK NCSC agentic-attack warning (24 Nov 2026)

items.title: France expects EU sanctions on 14 December over Iran’s refrigeration sabotage, after CISA and the FBI warned the threat to internet-connected controllers is ongoing
items.content_text: Hackers tampered with web-managed refrigeration controllers at about 700 French sites in October, forcing defrost or heating cycles; French authorities report at least 15 fires, and Paris blames the IRGC’s Shahid Kaveh unit. A second wave on 1–2 November reached about 11 European countries, and on 5 November CISA and the FBI, with HHS, USDA and DOT, warned that the threat is ongoing. France’s foreign minister said on 17 November he expects EU sanctions on 14 December, and EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas has confirmed new Iran sanctions are being prepared; Iran rejects the accusations. Sweden’s NCSC says victims mainly ran older systems with weak passwords. No water utility is reported hit, but exposed controllers with weak passwords and contractor remote access describe many small water sites too (editorial assessment).

items.title: Attackers rooted unpatched Check Point gateways through PHP2Shell, planted backdoors and wiped a VMware host; the root flaw is now in KEV
items.content_text: Check Point Research said on 12 November that attackers exploited the PHP2Shell flaws on unpatched Check Point Mobile Access portals from 30 October, then used a local flaw (CVE-2026-123039) to become root. They planted backdoors, pivoted to a VMware ESXi host and ran a wiper. The first wave hit Israeli organizations, some destructively; a second wave from 2 November reached several countries without destruction. Attribution is unconfirmed (tooling resembles China-nexus UNC5221). CISA added the root flaw to KEV on 13 November. No OT victim is reported, but these firewalls often sit at the IT/OT boundary and ESXi often hosts HMIs and historians (editorial assessment).

items.title: A crew GreyNoise calls GT13 breached Check Point management servers at 22 or more organizations, including energy and transport operators
items.content_text: GreyNoise reported, and Cybersecurity Dive covered on 24 November, that a campaign it tracks as GreyNoise13 (GT13) compromised at least 22 organizations in the UK, US, France, Germany, Australia, China and India between 17 October and 2 November, when GreyNoise lost direct visibility; it believes attempts continue. Victims are in energy, transportation, financial services and government. The crew exploited a Check Point SmartConsole/Security Management Server authentication bypass (CVE-2026-16232, patched in July) plus older Citrix NetScaler, Ivanti, Windows Netlogon and Rejetto HFS flaws, then moved laterally with Impacket, Chisel and Paramiko. GreyNoise has not linked GT13 to a known group or country, and says it is unrelated to the PHP2Shell gateway attacks. No water victim or OT impact is reported; it matters because utilities manage their firewalls from these servers (editorial assessment).

items.title: US officials eye Iran in up to 50 cyberattacks on energy tankers, widening the campaign that has already hit small water systems
items.content_text: US officials told the Wall Street Journal, in a report carried on 23–24 November, that Iran is the main suspect in as many as 50 cyberattacks on tankers carrying oil, liquefied gas and chemicals. The Coast Guard has sent cyber teams to at least four vessels nearing US shores, including the Texas-bound VL Prosperity and Kohaku, and the VL Prosperity’s captain received a ransom note. Some officials also name Russia, one administration official called four of the attacks a minor nuisance, and no ship is reported disabled. Water is not a target in this report, but it is the same period and, officials suspect, the same state sponsor as the water-station lockouts in the top story. Water utilities should expect the same tactics against their own exposed controllers and edge firewalls (editorial assessment).

items.title: A new water supply-chain index finds almost twice the vulnerabilities public records show, including 20 exploited flaws missing from CISA’s KEV list
items.content_text: Securin’s Water Supply Chain Watch, reported by The Register on 25 November, compared data on 236 technology vendors serving US drinking-water, wastewater and industrial-water systems against CISA, EPA, FBI and WaterISAC records. It found almost twice as many vulnerabilities as public records identify, including 20 exploited flaws that are not in CISA’s KEV catalog. Five vendors account for about half of 376 water-tagged advisories: Rockwell Automation, Advantech, Schneider Electric, Siemens and ABB. Securin also counted 791 internet-exposed Rockwell MicroLogix 1400 controllers as of 17 November, the model family hit in this summer’s water-utility attacks. Utilities that patch only from the KEV list will miss exploited flaws in their own gear, and exposed controllers remain the easiest way in (editorial assessment).

items.title: Lumen: Volt Typhoon’s “Silent Train” network has reached targets since 2023 through hijacked routers and flaws in management platforms, and lists water among the sectors hit
items.content_text: Lumen’s Black Lotus Labs reported on 28 October on Silent Train, a framework it attributes to Volt Typhoon, which US agencies link to the Chinese state, in use since November 2023. For each operation the operators build a single-use chain of overseas servers and hijacked home-office routers and IoT devices, sometimes in under two minutes, then take it apart, making the traffic hard to trace or block. Lumen ties the group to exploitation of Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN (CVE-2026-20127, CVSS v3.1 10.0), VeloCloud Orchestrator (CVE-2026-16812), N-able N-central (CVE-2025-8875, CVE-2025-8876), Versa Director and likely an undisclosed Quest KACE flaw. Its findings list water among affected sectors; Lumen has notified hundreds of victims over three years, most in Hawaii, California and Texas. No victim or OT intrusion is described. A compromised management platform reaches every site at once (editorial assessment).

items.title: Dragos counts 1,266 industrial ransomware attacks in Q3, four of them at water utilities, and found no operator touching a control system
items.content_text: Dragos said on 16 November that ransomware hit 1,266 industrial organizations between July and September 2026, up 11% from 1,140 in the second quarter, and the number of brands claiming industrial victims rose from 70 to 99. Manufacturing took 69% of cases; Dragos lists four water-utility incidents and seven at electric utilities. Qilin and The Gentlemen led the claims. Dragos found no Q3 case of a ransomware operator manipulating a control system: production stopped because the IT, ERP and virtualization layers that plants depend on went down, as when Fairlife halted all four of its US plants for about 11 days. Entry came through edge devices and enterprise applications exploited within days of disclosure, and through stolen VPN and firewall credentials. For utilities, the practical risk is losing billing, SCADA servers or historians hosted on shared IT infrastructure (editorial assessment).

items.title: Indiana water utilities weigh PLC exposure against small budgets as a state law extends cyber duties to systems serving 500 people
items.content_text: An Indianapolis Business Journal feature, republished by The Republic on 14 November, looks at how Indiana water and wastewater utilities handle cyber risk. Senate Enrolled Act 459 (2025) requires covered utilities to run annual cybersecurity evaluations, name a state cybersecurity contact and report incidents, and lowers the threshold to systems serving at least 500 people from 3,300. A lawyer quoted estimates that about 80% of water infrastructure is run by local governments with few dedicated security staff; Tipton pays about $25,000 up front and $5,000 a year for contracted security. The state’s drinking-water cybersecurity lead said one activity reported during the summer campaign caused no disruption and may have been federal scanning. Interviewees named exposed PLCs as the main risk and warned that falsified monitoring data could trigger responses to conditions that are not happening.

items.title: Claroty finds 65,000 game consoles, smart speakers and cars on critical-infrastructure networks, most of them on production segments
items.content_text: Claroty said on 17 November that, across 45 million devices at more than 30,000 critical-infrastructure sites, it found about 65,000 consumer gadgets that do not belong on operational networks: game consoles, smart-home and entertainment devices, and connected cars. Industrial sites had 963 game consoles, nearly 90% of them on production rather than guest networks, and thousands of connected vehicles were attached to site networks with almost none isolated on a guest segment. Claroty did not break the figures out for water utilities. At treatment plants and pump stations where the plant network, office Wi-Fi and staff devices share switches, each unmanaged gadget is a foothold that quietly undermines the segmentation SCADA depends on (editorial assessment).

items.title: PHP2Shell attacks rooted about two dozen Palo Alto firewalls, and Siemens, Schneider and ABB now list grid-control, DCS and RTU products, several with no fix
items.content_text: Palo Alto’s Unit 42 verified that a suspected China-nexus actor chained the PHP2Shell flaws (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619) with Linux kernel bug CVE-2026-46300 to root about two dozen internet-exposed PAN-OS firewalls on 23–24 October and steal Active Directory credentials. Siemens (Spectrum Power, AMIS TS and, since 16 November, WTV676/WTV776 metering gateways), Schneider (a Foxboro DCS server) and ABB (Netcontrol RTUs, ASPECT gateways) now list affected products, several unfixed. None is reported exploited and no OT operator is named: treat it as an IT-to-OT boundary warning.

items.title: A vCenter authentication bypass was exploited as a zero-day for two months before Broadcom’s 19 November patch; vCenter 7.0 gets no fix
items.content_text: Broadcom patched CVE-2026-123890 on 19 November, a critical flaw in vCenter’s directory service that gives a remote, unauthenticated attacker an administrator session. Google’s Mandiant, which reported it, says a suspected China-linked espionage group it tracks as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221, also called Warp Panda) exploited it for more than two months beforehand. In the cases investigated, the group entered through a BeyondTrust Remote Support flaw, attacked vCenter in early September with a custom tool called Bonesaw, stole SAML signing material and the vCenter master key, forged tokens and moved to ESXi hosts. Fixes are in vCenter 9.1.1.0200, 9.0.2.0200 and 8.0 U3m; end-of-life vCenter 7.0 has no public patch. No victims or sectors are named. Many plants run HMIs and historians as virtual machines, so whoever controls vCenter controls them (editorial assessment).
tags: Active exploitation — VMware vCenter authentication bypass CVE-2026-123890 (CVSS 9.8) exploited as a zero-day for more than two months by a suspected China-linked group, per Mandiant; Broadcom fix released 19 Nov 2026; no public fix for vCenter 7.0

items.title: N-able ships Hotfix 3 for 17 more N-central flaws after attackers planted miners on servers already running Hotfix 2
items.content_text: N-able released N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 3 on 16 November as a critical security update. It fixes 17 new CVEs, including authentication bypasses, path traversal leading to code execution and a syslog injection that runs commands as root, and removes the Legacy API option that the actively exploited 4EverAble2Shell chain depends on. On-premises servers need the upgrade now; hosted servers update automatically, but every customer must also upgrade Agents and Probes, which can otherwise be impersonated. The fix follows Huntback’s 13 November finding of cryptocurrency miners on 21 N-central servers, 19 on Hotfix 2. Separately, N-able said on 20 November that attackers reached a server in its hosted Mail Assure and SpamExperts cloud; it found no access to customer data and says the breach is unrelated to N-central. Integrators often manage plant-side Windows hosts through RMM tools (editorial assessment).

items.title: Attackers root clustered Cisco Expressway gateways soon after a public exploit, and CISA adds the flaw to KEV
items.content_text: Security firm F6 says attackers exploited CVE-2026-76466, a critical flaw in clustered Cisco Expressway Core and Edge deployments, shortly after proof-of-concept code appeared on GitHub. They broke into two internet-facing Expressway nodes at an unnamed Russian organization, moved to more cluster nodes inside the network and gained root, then ran scripts to scan for SMB shares, SQL Server and WinRM hosts and to hunt for credentials. CISA added the flaw to its KEV catalog on 20 November. Cisco fixed it on 21 October; there is no workaround. No water utility or OT victim is reported. Larger utilities and city IT departments that run Expressway for remote calling should treat an exposed, unpatched cluster as a foothold close to SCADA and plant networks (editorial assessment; cross-sector item carried for water).

items.title: Java4Shell exploitation attempts begin, and Siemens tells customers to take Industrial Edge Management offline until patched
items.content_text: Probing for Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), a memory-corruption bug in how OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later decode Base64 data, started within two days of its 17 November disclosure. GreyNoise counted more than 150 matching requests from five addresses by early 19 November and Previdian logged nine attempts from six addresses; none is confirmed to have succeeded. Exploitation needs a recent Intel or AMD x86-64 processor with AVX-512 VBMI, and researchers at Calif showed unauthenticated code execution against default Jira, Confluence, Jenkins and Keycloak setups, each with a tailored chain. For OT teams the key item is Siemens advisory SSA-272816: three Industrial Edge Management products are affected, fixes are in progress, and Siemens recommends taking those instances offline until they are patched. Cisco lists more than a dozen products with no fix yet, and Atlassian Data Center products are also unpatched.

items.title: CISA warns a crafted project file can run code on engineering laptops through AutomationDirect’s C-More EA9 HMI software
items.content_text: CISA published ICSA-26-328-01 on 24 November for AutomationDirect’s C-More EA9 programming software, versions 6.80 and earlier. CVE-2026-127280 (CVSS 7.8) is a heap-based buffer overflow: opening a maliciously crafted project file can let an attacker run code on the engineering workstation. CISA lists manufacturing, energy and water and wastewater among the affected sectors and reports no known public exploitation. C-More touch panels are common in small treatment plants, lift stations and skid packages, where project files are often passed between integrators and operators by email or USB (editorial assessment). The risk sits on the laptop that builds and downloads HMI screens, not the panel itself.

items.title: November ICS patches: Siemens flags high-severity flaws in SIMATIC SCADA, PCS 7 and WinCC Graphics Designer, several without fixes, plus Node2Shell exposure
items.content_text: Siemens published nine advisories covering ten vulnerabilities on November’s ICS Patch Tuesday, SecurityWeek reported on 11 November. High-severity issues affect SIMATIC SCADA and PCS 7, SIMATIC WinCC Graphics Designer, IOT2050, ROS#, Simcenter Femap and the Mendix Studio Pro MCP server; patches are not yet available for several products, and some versions will never be fixed. Two more advisories cover Node2Shell (CVE-2026-111497), a Brotli decoder flaw in Node.js that CISA added to KEV on 27 October; exploitation attempts have been seen, none aimed at Siemens products. CISA republished the Brotli assessment as ICSA-26-321-03 on 17 November, naming WinCC V7/V8, WinCC Runtime Professional, WinCC OA and TIA Administrator; fixes exist only for BRAUMAT/SISTAR and WinCC OA V3.20, so most WinCC sites must disable Brotli for now. WinCC and PCS 7 run HMI and SCADA screens at many water plants (editorial assessment).

items.title: The Water Watch Center now gives free security monitoring and help to water utilities in 26 states
items.content_text: The Water Watch Center, a joint effort of the National Rural Water Association and the volunteer hacker group DEF CON Franklin, said on Friday 20 November that it is providing free security monitoring and assistance to water utilities in 26 states, Cybersecurity Dive reported on 23 November. Launched in August, the center pays security firms, including Rapid7, Defendify, Legato Security, TPO Group and BlastWave, to give rural utilities free intrusion detection and defensive consultations. Nearly 100 utilities have contacted it so far. It is funded by grants from Craig Newmark Philanthropies, the Hewlett Foundation and DARPA. For small systems with no security staff it is one of the few no-cost ways to get eyes on the network; the limit is staff time to install sensors and act on alerts (editorial assessment).

items.title: Texas Cyber Command signs up 63 companies to give Texas water and wastewater utilities free security help under Project Watershed 250
items.content_text: Texas Cyber Command has brought 63 technology and cybersecurity companies into Project Watershed 250, the six-month pilot launched on 31 August by the White House Office of the National Cyber Director with the Texas governor’s office, GovTech reported on 18 November. Partners named include Palo Alto Networks, Cisco, Cloudflare, Akamai, Tenable, AWS, Claroty and Elisity, covering OT and ICS visibility, enterprise security tools, assessments and remediation at no cost; utilities choose which services to use, and Dispel said on 19 November it is offering OT remote access. Texas has about 7,400 public water systems and 3,000 wastewater treatment facilities. No participation numbers or results have been published, and partners are still working out what can be delivered quickly and how services continue after the pilot.

items.title: Comments close 30 November on NIST’s draft rewrite of its OT security guide, which adds water, food, rail, maritime and building-automation coverage
items.content_text: NIST’s draft Revision 4 of SP 800-82, the US government’s main guide to operational technology security, is open for public comment until 30 November 2026. The draft reorganises the guide around Cybersecurity Framework 2.0, with risk management now led by the Govern function, and adds sector material for building automation, water and wastewater, food and agriculture, freight rail, maritime vessels, and industrial IoT connected to cloud services. It also expands guidance on asset management, network monitoring and detection, protecting system-management functions, and applying zero-trust principles. Many regulators, insurers and auditors use 800-82 as a reference, so its final wording can shape what operators are asked to show; the comment window is the chance for practitioners to flag guidance that would not work on a plant floor.
